definition: The property that accesses respect object bounds, valid lifetimes and permitted memory operations. Ordinary raw-pointer operations in C/C++ do not universally enforce it, so memory-safety bugs can corrupt or disclose data.
example: Chromium reported that around 70% of a sample of 912 high or critical security bugs since 2015 were memory-safety bugs.

definition: Behaviour for which the C or C++ standard imposes no requirements, such as writing past an array or using freed memory. The program might crash, appear to work, or do something an attacker can steer; compilers may also optimise on the assumption it never happens.
example: strcpy into an 8-byte buffer from an 11-byte source has undefined behaviour: no particular crash or overwrite is promised.

definition: The international standard that defines the C programming language. C99, C11 and C17 are editions from 1999, 2011 and 2018 (C17 mostly fixes C11); they say which operations are valid and which have undefined behaviour.
example: The function gets was removed from the library in C11 because it cannot be used safely.

definition: A general-purpose language with classes, templates and low-level memory operations. It shares much syntax and some library interfaces with C, but is a separate language; ordinary raw-pointer operations do not universally enforce object bounds or lifetimes.

A value holding the memory address of something else, such as a buffer or a function. In C, code can do arithmetic on pointers and follow them without the language checking that the target is still valid.
example: If p points to the start of char buf[16], then p + 15 points at its last byte and p + 16 is one past the end.

definition: A test that an index or length lies inside the object being accessed before the access happens. C does not perform them automatically; the programmer must write them.
example: Before copying len bytes into a 16-byte buffer, check that len ≤ 16.

definition: The period during which an object's storage is validly reserved for it, for example from malloc until free. Using the object outside its lifetime is a temporal memory-safety bug.
example: After free(s), the lifetime of *s has ended. C makes pointers to that ended object indeterminate; do not inspect or dereference them as if they were valid addresses.

definition: A memory-safety bug where an access falls outside the object's bounds, such as a buffer overflow or an out-of-bounds read. The question it breaks is 'is this address inside the object?'.
example: Writing arr[10] in a 10-element array is a spatial error: valid indices are 0 to 9.

definition: A memory-safety bug where an access happens outside the object's lifetime, such as use-after-free or double free. The address may once have been valid, but the object is no longer alive.
example: Reading s->name after free(s) is a temporal error.

definition: An unintended change to memory caused by a bug, such as an overflow writing over neighbouring data. Attackers use it to alter decisions or redirect execution.

How a running program's memory is arranged: code, global data, the heap and the stack placed in separate regions of its address space. Exact placement depends on the operating system, architecture and ASLR.

Storage used to keep track of active function calls on many implementations. Some locals, saved registers and return information may be stored there; registers, optimisation and the calling convention determine the actual layout.
example: A conventional unoptimised greet call can use a frame holding buf[16]; optimisation and the ABI determine whether those objects and a separate frame remain.

definition: Storage associated with one active function call, often including spilled values, locals or saved state. Its contents and even whether a separate frame exists depend on the architecture, calling convention and compiler.

Dynamically allocated storage obtained through interfaces such as malloc in C or new in C++. It can occupy multiple mappings; allocated objects remain alive until released through the appropriate mechanism.
example: malloc(64) returns a pointer to 64 bytes of heap memory.

definition: Common program-image sections for initialised data and zero-initialised storage. Their actual permissions come from the loaded mappings; a section name alone does not guarantee that a page is non-executable.
The region of a program image that holds its machine code. It is normally mapped readable and executable but not writable.

Register values stored so a function can restore them when required by its calling convention. Some are kept in a stack frame; exact registers and storage locations depend on the ABI and generated code.

The location execution should resume after a function call. Architectures may keep it in a link register or on a stack; corrupting stored return information can redirect a later return when no effective check stops it.
example: On x86-64, call pushes the 8-byte return address and ret pops it into the instruction pointer.

definition: A register used as a stable reference for a function's stack frame in some calling conventions. Compilers may omit it; saving and restoring it and unwinding frames depend on the ABI and generated code.

A variable declared in a local scope. A local can have automatic, static or thread storage duration; ordinary non-static function locals usually have automatic duration and may be held in registers or on the stack.
The library code behind malloc and free that hands out heap memory and recycles freed blocks. Its choices about when to reuse memory decide how a use-after-free plays out.
example: glibc's malloc keeps freed chunks on free lists and can hand the same address to the next malloc of a similar size.

definition: Bookkeeping an allocator uses to manage storage, such as sizes and free-list links. Its location and protection depend on the allocator; corrupting it can cause failures or exploitable behaviour without guaranteeing a particular write.

Values used to determine control transfers, such as stored return addresses and function pointers. Corrupting them can redirect execution if the resulting transfer is possible and effective protections do not reject it.
The order in which a program's instructions execute, including calls, returns, jumps and branches.
An attack that corrupts control data, such as a return address or function pointer, so the program jumps to a location of the attacker's choosing.

An attack that corrupts ordinary program data, such as an authorisation flag, without needing an unintended control-flow transfer. Protections limited to return or indirect-branch integrity do not generally validate that data.
example: A possible threat scenario is an overflow from name[16] affecting a neighbouring is_admin decision without changing a return address; the invalid C copy has no guaranteed outcome.

definition: A write outside a buffer's bounds, before its start or beyond its end. In C this is undefined behaviour: corrupting nearby data, crashing or redirecting execution are possible risks, not guaranteed traces.
example: Copying a 40-byte name with strcpy needs 41 bytes including NUL, exceeding char buf[16] by 25; the invalid call has no promised overwrite trace.

definition: An out-of-bounds write involving a buffer stored on a call stack. It may affect nearby state or saved control information depending on the generated layout; C does not guarantee a particular overwrite or outcome.

A write proceeding through consecutive locations beyond a buffer boundary. In a protected layout where a canary lies between that buffer and saved return information, reaching the latter crosses the guard; layouts and detection are not universal.

A memory write that lands at a chosen location without touching the bytes in between, for example arr[i] = x with an attacker-controlled index i. It can change a return address while leaving the stack canary intact.
Reading memory outside the object being accessed. If the bytes reach the attacker, it discloses memory, possibly secrets or addresses that weaken ASLR; Heartbleed is the famous case.
example: Heartbleed copied up to 65,535 bytes from a payload that might only be a few bytes long.

definition: A bug where a loop or bound is wrong by exactly one, for example using <= instead of <. With arrays it typically reads or writes one element past the end.
example: for (i = 0; i <= 8; i++) on char id[8] writes id[8], one past the last valid index 7.

definition: An information disclosure that reveals a pointer value. If the corresponding build and relative offset are known, it can identify the base of that particular fixed-layout mapping; it does not automatically reveal other mappings.
A byte whose value is 0. As a character it is called NUL, written '\0' in C; C strings end at the first NUL, so string functions copy or read until they meet one.
example: "abc" occupies 4 bytes: 'a', 'b', 'c' and a NUL.

definition: A sequence of characters ending with a NUL byte. Operations expecting a C string require a reachable terminator within valid storage; an unterminated array does not satisfy that contract.

The C library function strcpy(dst, src) copies a valid NUL-terminated source including its NUL into a sufficiently large, non-overlapping destination. It has no destination-capacity argument; violating those requirements gives undefined behaviour.
example: Copying "ABCDEFGHIJ" needs 11 bytes including NUL, exceeding char buf[8] by 3; no particular effect of that invalid call is promised.

definition: The C library function strncpy(dst, src, n) that copies at most n bytes. If the source is n bytes or longer it does not add a terminating NUL, and if shorter it pads the rest with NULs, so it is not a safe strcpy.
example: strncpy(dst, "abcdef", 4) leaves dst holding abcd with no NUL.

definition: A bounded string copy, from BSD and now in some other C libraries, that always NUL-terminates when the size is non-zero and returns the source's length so truncation can be detected. It is not part of ISO C, so it is not available everywhere.

A C formatting function that bounds output by the supplied capacity and, for valid arguments with non-zero capacity, writes a terminating NUL. A non-negative return gives the full required length excluding NUL; a negative return reports an encoding error.
example: snprintf(d, 8, "%s", "hello world") stores hello w and returns 11.

definition: The C library function that prints text according to a format string, replacing directives such as %s and %d with its further arguments. Passing untrusted text as the format string is the format-string bug.

A C library function formatting text into a destination without a capacity argument. The caller must provide enough valid storage for all output and its NUL; use snprintf with correct arguments and error/truncation handling to bound writes.

A C library function that writes a valid NUL-terminated string to a stream without interpreting percent-format directives. It still requires a valid string and stream and can report an output failure.
A C library function that copies a specified number of bytes between valid, non-overlapping ranges. The caller must ensure both ranges are large enough; use memmove for permitted overlap.
example: Heartbleed's bug was a memcpy whose n came from the attacker.

definition: A C library function like memcpy that copies n bytes but also works correctly when the source and destination overlap.
An old C library function that read a line of input into a buffer with no way to give the buffer's size, so any long line overflowed it. It was removed from the language in C11.

Cutting data off at a size limit, keeping only the first part, such as a string shortened to fit a buffer. In C, bounded functions such as snprintf truncate output that does not fit, and code must check for it because silently shortened data can itself cause bugs.
example: Formatting "hello world" into 8 bytes truncates it to hello w.

definition: The unsigned integer type C uses for object sizes and byte counts, returned by sizeof and taken by malloc. It is typically 32 bits on 32-bit platforms and 64 bits on 64-bit ones.
example: With a 32-bit size_t the largest value is 4,294,967,295.

definition: A C constant equal to the largest value size_t can hold: 2^32 − 1 (4,294,967,295) for a 32-bit size_t. Checking count > SIZE_MAX / size before multiplying detects size overflow.
A C operator giving the size of an object or type in C bytes. Many results are compile-time constants, but sizes involving variable-length arrays can be evaluated at run time.

Optional exact-width unsigned C types from <stdint.h>: uint8_t has 8 value bits, uint32_t 32 and uint64_t 64. On an eight-bit-byte implementation their sizes are one, four and eight bytes; an implementation need not provide every exact-width type.

An integer type representing non-negative values. Arithmetic performed in an unsigned type reduces results modulo one more than that type's maximum; integer promotions may first move smaller operands to another type.
example: A 32-bit unsigned value holds 0 to 4,294,967,295.

definition: An arithmetic result outside the representable range of its intended type. C unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo the type's range, while signed overflow is normally undefined behaviour; either can undermine size calculations.
example: With a 32-bit size_t, 268,435,457 × 16 wraps to 16.

definition: What an unsigned integer does when a result leaves its range: it keeps only the lowest bits, so counting continues from 0 after the maximum (and from the maximum below 0). For a 32-bit type this is arithmetic modulo 2^32.
example: In 32-bit unsigned arithmetic, 4,294,967,295 + 1 gives 0 and 0 − 1 gives 4,294,967,295.

definition: Subtracting more than an unsigned value holds, so the result wraps around to a huge number instead of going negative. A length check written as len > total − 19 is fooled when total is below 19.
example: With a 32-bit size_t, 10 − 19 gives 4,294,967,287.

definition: The prefix C and most programming tools put before a hexadecimal number, so 0x10 means sixteen rather than ten.

An architecture-dependent natural unit for registers and operations, whose meaning depends on context. x86-64 has 64-bit general-purpose registers; the illustrated glibc guard is a uintptr_t, eight bytes in the conventional 64-bit ABI. Other ABIs can use smaller pointers.
A byte order in which the least significant byte of a multi-byte value is stored at the lowest address. x86-64 and most Arm systems are little-endian.
example: The 4-byte value 0x11223344 is stored as 44 33 22 11.

definition: A temporal memory-safety bug in which a program keeps using a pointer after the memory it points to has been freed. If the allocator has reused that memory for attacker-controlled data, the stale access can read or act on it.
example: A possible threat scenario is a freed session's storage being reused for request bytes before a stale alias is accessed; C does not guarantee what the invalid access observes.

definition: Freeing the same allocation twice, which is undefined behaviour in C. It can corrupt the allocator's bookkeeping or make two later allocations share memory; some allocators detect it and abort.

A pointer formerly associated with an object whose lifetime has ended, such as storage released by free. C can make the pointer value indeterminate when the object ends; later use is not a portable way to access any replacement object.
Another pointer referring to the same object. Setting one pointer to NULL does not alter its aliases; if the object is freed, those aliases no longer provide valid access to that object.

A convention or language mechanism specifying who releases an allocation and how borrowing or shared lifetime is managed. Correctly maintained ownership prevents stale access and duplicate release, but a stated convention alone does not enforce it.

A move-only C++ smart pointer holding exclusive ownership through an associated deleter. Destruction or reset invokes that deleter for its managed object; release instead transfers the stored pointer without destroying the object. Borrowed aliases still need lifetime discipline.

A C++ smart pointer sharing ownership through a control block. The managed object is destroyed when the last owning shared_ptr releases it; weak_ptr references may keep the control block storage alive for longer.
A pointer value that points to no object. free(NULL) does nothing, but dereferencing NULL is undefined behaviour, not a guaranteed clean crash.
To follow a pointer and access the object at its address, such as reading s->is_admin through the pointer s.
The C library function that allocates a block of heap memory of a given number of bytes and returns a pointer to it, or NULL on failure. The block must later be released with free.
example: malloc(count * 16) requests 16 bytes per item, unless the multiplication wraps.

definition: A C library function that allocates memory for count items of a given size and zeroes it. glibc's calloc returns NULL instead of wrapping when count × size overflows.
A function, standardised in POSIX but not ISO C, that resizes an array allocation for count items of a given size and fails instead of wrapping when count × size overflows.

Access to shared state without sufficient coordination. In C/C++, conflicting actions in different threads, at least one non-atomic and neither ordered before the other by happens-before, constitute a data race and give undefined behaviour.
A bug where untrusted text is passed as the format argument of printf or a similar function, so % directives in it are interpreted. It can disclose memory or, with %n, attempt a write.
example: printf(user_input) with input %x %x %x may print stack values.

definition: A %-sequence in a printf format string. Conversions such as %s, %d and %x consume arguments of specified types, and %n stores the emitted character count through a pointer; %% instead emits a literal percent sign without consuming an argument.

Platform rules for passing arguments, returning results and preserving registers. Supplying missing or wrongly typed printf arguments violates its contract; a particular leak or output is not portable.
A variable read before anything has been stored in it. In C an uninitialised local has an indeterminate value, and many uses of it are undefined behaviour rather than a reliable read of old bytes.

Bytes between or after structure members that are not part of those members, commonly needed for alignment. C gives padding unspecified values when structure or member values are stored, so member assignments do not establish safe contents for a raw copy across a trust boundary.
example: In struct { uint8_t flag; uint64_t value; }, bytes 1–7 are typically padding, making the struct 16 bytes.

definition: The requirement that a value of a given type starts at an address that is a multiple of some number, often its own size. A uint64_t is typically 8-byte aligned, which is why padding appears before it.
An explicitly defined layout of bytes for sending data between programs, with set field sizes, order and endianness, independent of how a compiler lays out a struct in memory.

A Linux kernel helper for copying a specified number of bytes to user space, with user-access checks. It can fail or copy only part of the requested range; the caller must also ensure that the source bytes are appropriate to disclose.
Code that runs inside the operating-system kernel to control hardware or provide a service. Bugs in it run with the kernel's full privileges.
The memory and privilege level where ordinary programs run, separated from the kernel. Data passes between them only through controlled interfaces such as system calls.
A widely used open-source operating-system kernel; GNU/Linux refers to it together with the GNU tools and C library (glibc).

A 2014 OpenSSL vulnerability (CVE-2014-0160): the TLS heartbeat code trusted the length an attacker claimed and copied that many bytes back, leaking up to about 64 KB of server memory per request, including possible private keys and cookies.

Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a programme assigning identifiers and publishing records for publicly disclosed vulnerabilities. A CVE ID such as CVE-2014-0160 identifies one record; not every known vulnerability necessarily has an ID or a published record.

A TLS extension (RFC 6520) for checking a connection is alive: one side sends a payload and the other echoes it back. A message holds a 1-byte type, a 2-byte payload length, the payload and at least 16 bytes of padding.

The part of a message header that says how long the message's payload (or the whole message) is. For example, in a TLS heartbeat it is 2 bytes counting only the payload, so it can claim up to 65,535 bytes; it must be checked against what actually arrived.

Code that reads structured input, such as a file format or network message, and turns it into data the program uses. Parsers of untrusted input are a prime source of memory-safety bugs and a prime fuzzing target.

A compiler-inserted memory-error detector in Clang and GCC, enabled with -fsanitize=address. It marks memory around and after objects as poisoned in shadow memory and reports accesses to it, catching many overflows and use-after-free bugs on the paths a test runs.
example: ASan reports heap-use-after-free when code reads an object that is still in its freed quarantine.

definition: A Clang and GCC run-time checker that reports certain kinds of undefined behaviour when they happen, such as signed integer overflow or misaligned pointers.
A compiler feature that adds run-time checks to a program to detect a class of bugs while it runs, such as AddressSanitizer for memory errors. It finds bugs only on the paths actually executed.
A separate region of memory that records metadata about the program's own memory. AddressSanitizer uses one shadow byte per 8 application bytes to record which bytes are safe to access.
Marking memory as off-limits, for example the gaps around objects and recently freed blocks, so a checker such as ASan reports any access to it.
A checker or allocator holding freed memory back for a while before handing it out again, so a use-after-free hits poisoned memory and is detected instead of reaching a new object.

Additional code or runtime machinery used to observe or check a program. Coverage depends on the mechanism; compiler instrumentation and intercepted library operations can detect different accesses, and gaps can leave bugs undetected.

A tool that runs an unmodified program on a simulated CPU, checking each memory access for errors such as use of freed or uninitialised memory. It needs no recompilation but makes the program much slower.
Adding checks to a compiled program's machine code while it runs, without its source code, as Valgrind does.
Automatically running a program on large numbers of generated or mutated inputs, often malformed, to find crashes and bugs. Combined with sanitizers it exposes memory errors on the paths it reaches.

Fuzzing that uses execution feedback, such as newly reached code, to choose useful inputs for further mutation. It can improve exploration but does not guarantee deeper coverage or discovery of every bug.
An in-process, coverage-guided fuzzing engine that is part of LLVM. You write a small function that passes each generated input to the code under test.
A widely used coverage-guided fuzzer, the community successor to American Fuzzy Lop (AFL).
A free Google service that continuously fuzzes eligible open-source projects with sanitizers and reports the bugs it finds to their maintainers.
A collection of sample inputs, such as valid image files, used as tests or as the starting point that a fuzzer mutates.
A test kept to check that behaviour which used to work, or a bug that was fixed, does not break again.
Analysis of a program without executing its normal workload. Tools approximate possible behaviour and can report false positives or miss bugs; their guarantees depend on the analysis and assumptions.

GCC and Clang options: -Wall turns on a broad set of common warnings (including -Wformat); -Wformat checks printf-style calls against their format strings; -Wformat-security warns when a non-literal format string has no arguments; and -Werror (or -Werror=format-security) turns warnings into build errors.
An option passed to the compiler or linker on its command line, such as -O2 or -fstack-protector-strong, that changes how a program is built.

How hard the compiler works to make code faster or smaller: -O0 means no optimisation, while -O1 to -O3 enable increasingly aggressive optimisation. Some checks, such as FORTIFY_SOURCE, need optimisation to work.

The GNU Compiler Collection, an open-source compiler collection supporting C, C++ and other languages. Its flags and enabled protections depend on the compiler version, target and build configuration.
The C, C++ and Objective-C compiler of the LLVM project. It provides sanitizers and control-flow integrity schemes.

The GNU C Library, a C library implementation used by GNU/Linux systems. It provides interfaces such as malloc, strcpy and printf, and implementation support for stack guards and source fortification. Other Linux systems can use another C library.

A C library implementation providing interfaces such as malloc, printf and memcpy. It can be linked dynamically or statically; glibc is one GNU/Linux implementation. Known code in a loaded library may be used by code-reuse attacks.
Portable Operating System Interface: an IEEE standard for Unix-like system interfaces, adding functions such as reallocarray that ISO C does not define.
The signal a Unix-like operating system sends a process that touches memory it may not access, which normally terminates it. A crash, not a guaranteed result of a memory bug.
A protection in the compiler, operating system or CPU that makes particular ways of exploiting a bug harder, such as stack canaries or ASLR. It does not fix the bug itself.
Configuring software, its build or a system so that bugs are harder to exploit, for example by enabling stack protection, RELRO and fortification.
The set of programs that turn source code into a running program: compiler, assembler, linker and C library.

A guard checked by generated code on protected function exits. In a conventional layout it lies between local buffers and saved return information, so a linear overwrite crossing it may be detected; coverage and layout depend on the compiler and ABI.
example: With glibc on x86-64 the canary is 8 bytes with its lowest byte set to zero, leaving 56 random bits.

definition: The function that stack-protector code calls when a canary check fails. In glibc it reports stack smashing and aborts the process.

GCC options that insert stack guards in selected functions. The basic option covers functions with alloca or sufficiently large stack buffers; the strong option also includes local arrays and local-frame-address references, considering objects that remain on the stack after optimisation.
The instructions at the end of a function that restore saved registers and return to the caller. With stack protection, the canary check runs here, just before ret.

A 2014 attack technique (Bittau et al., 'Hacking Blind') against servers that restart crashed workers with the same memory layout. It reads the canary and return addresses a byte at a time from crash or no-crash responses, then builds return-oriented programming chains.

A POSIX operation creating a child process with an initially copied address space. The child initially inherits mapping locations and guard values in copied memory; later runtime actions or executing a new program can change them.

A protection that marks memory pages as non-executable, so the CPU refuses to run instructions from data areas such as the stack and heap. NX is the hardware page bit; DEP is Microsoft's name for the feature.
example: Injected machine code on a non-executable stack page faults when the CPU tries to fetch it.

definition: A policy prohibiting simultaneous write and execute permission for a mapping. Stronger variants also address writable aliases of executable storage; ordinary NX alone only blocks execution from pages marked non-executable.
The fixed-size block, typically 4 KiB on x86-64 Linux, in which the operating system maps memory and sets read, write and execute permissions.
The read, write and execute rights set for each memory page. The CPU checks them on every access and faults on a violation.
The CPU reading the next machine instruction from memory before executing it. NX makes this fail on pages not marked executable.
Instructions encoded as bytes the CPU executes directly.
Placing the attacker's own machine code in memory, for example in a buffer, and redirecting execution to it. NX blocks it on non-executable pages.
An attack that redirects execution through instructions already in the program and its libraries instead of injecting new code. Because that code is legitimately executable, NX does not stop it.
A code-reuse attack that places a chain of addresses on the stack, each pointing to a short existing instruction sequence ending in ret, so each return runs the next piece of the attacker's program.

An existing instruction sequence ending in a return, used as a building block in a return-oriented program. Which operations an attacker can compose depends on the available sequences, controllable state and effective protections.
example: A gadget such as pop rdi; ret lets the attacker load a chosen value into a register.

definition: In x86, an instruction returning from a function by taking the return address from the ordinary stack, with additional checks when features such as CET shadow stacks are enabled. Other architectures can use a return instruction that takes its target from a register instead.

A just-in-time compiler: it turns code into machine code while the program runs, as JavaScript engines do. It therefore needs memory that becomes executable at run time, which must be protected carefully.
A second, writable mapping of memory that is also mapped executable elsewhere. An attacker who can write through it can change code that will run, undermining W^X.

Address space layout randomisation: platform policy that varies placement of selected mappings. Coverage and entropy depend on support and configuration; knowing a build-specific pointer offset can reveal a particular mapping base.
example: With 28 random bits a library can start at any of 268,435,456 positions.

definition: The range of memory addresses a process can use, each mapped by the operating system to physical memory or nothing. Each process has its own.
An address-space region associated with backing storage and access permissions. ASLR may randomise the placement of selected mappings; not every region must move or be independently placed.

The starting address used to describe a mapping or loaded object. For a known fixed-layout image, known relative offsets locate targets from that base; independently allocated or specially resolved objects may need different reasoning.

A distance from a specified origin, usually measured in bytes for a structure field or mapped image. Adding a known target's relative offset to the matching fixed-layout image base locates it; separately allocated or specially resolved objects need different reasoning.
A Linux setting (sysctl) that chooses how many random bits ASLR uses for the base of mmap-allocated regions, within limits the architecture and kernel build allow.
A Linux interface for reading and changing kernel settings at run time, such as vm.mmap_rnd_bits.
Kernel address space layout randomisation: loading the operating-system kernel itself at a random address at boot. A leaked kernel pointer can reveal the base.

Chosen so that every possible value has the same probability. Independent means each choice is unaffected by the others. Together these assumptions underpin many simple estimates, such as average-case search costs, hash-collision odds and 2^b guessing estimates for b random bits.
The long-run average of a random quantity, such as the number of guesses an attack needs, over many repetitions.
example: Guessing one of 256 fixed candidates in order takes 128.5 attempts on average.

definition: The probability distribution of how many independent tries it takes to get the first success when each try succeeds with probability p. Its mean is 1/p.
example: With a 1-in-256 chance per try, the mean is 256 tries.

definition: Executable and Linkable Format: the file format for programs and shared libraries on Linux and most other Unix-like systems.

A position-independent executable, built so the main image can run at different load addresses. Random placement still requires loader and OS policy; conventional non-PIE ELF main-code addresses are generally fixed.

Relocation Read-Only: a supported ELF linker/loader arrangement that protects a designated relocation region after processing. Full RELRO also uses eager function binding so the conventional GOT layout can be made read-only; other pointers remain unprotected.

Adjusting address-dependent values when code or data is placed at its final location. Linkers can apply relocations while producing an executable, and dynamic loaders apply the relevant remaining relocations when objects are loaded.

Global Offset Table: an ELF mechanism holding addresses used by generated code, including data and function references. Redirecting a writable relevant entry can affect accesses or calls; full RELRO protects the covered entries in a conventional supported layout.
Resolving an external function's address only on its first call, which needs the GOT entry to stay writable while the program runs.

aliases: resolved when the object is loaded
definition: Resolving all of a program's required function addresses when it is loaded instead of on first call, requested with the linker flag -z now. It lets the GOT be made read-only before main runs.
A compiler option that passes -z relro and -z now to the linker (-Wl, means 'pass to the linker'), enabling full RELRO.
Conventional build variables (for example in Makefiles) holding the options passed to the C compiler (CFLAGS) and the linker (LDFLAGS).
The part of the system (ld.so on Linux) that maps a program and its shared libraries into memory at start-up, applies relocations and resolves function addresses.
A function that loads a shared library into a running process on request, after start-up. The new library has its own relocations.
A system call that changes the permissions (read, write, execute) of pages in a process's memory; the loader uses it to make the RELRO region read-only.

A glibc/compiler feature adding diagnostics and checks to supported library calls when suitable object-size information is available. Glibc enables its wrappers with optimisation; level 3 uses dynamic object sizes and requires compatible toolchain support.
example: memcpy(dst, src, n) becomes __memcpy_chk(dst, src, n, dst_size), which aborts if n > dst_size.

definition: Compiler built-ins that report how many bytes remain in the object a pointer points to, if the compiler can tell. _FORTIFY_SOURCE uses __builtin_object_size, and at level 3 __builtin_dynamic_object_size, which also handles run-time sizes.
The checked version of memcpy that fortified code calls: it takes the destination's size as an extra argument and aborts if the copy would exceed it.
Application binary interface: the low-level rules a platform's compiled code follows, such as type sizes, struct layout and alignment, calling convention and stack-frame layout.

The 64-bit extension of the x86 instruction-set architecture, implemented by Intel and AMD processors among others. It uses little-endian byte order; a chosen ABI determines the sizes of C types and pointers.

A family of protections that check indirect calls, jumps or returns go only to targets the program could legitimately reach, defeating many code-reuse attacks. Schemes differ in which transfers they check and how precisely.
In control-flow integrity, a transfer to a new location chosen at run time: an indirect call or jump. Forward-edge protections include Clang CFI, Microsoft CFG, Intel IBT and Arm BTI.

A return transfer from a function to its caller. Shadow stacks and selected pointer-authentication arrangements can protect stored return information; their coverage depends on enablement and code generation.

A call whose target is obtained at run time, for example from a function pointer. Indirect jumps also obtain their target at run time; corrupting a target can redirect execution or trigger a check or fault.

A pointer to a function, usable for indirect calls with a compatible type. Corrupting it can redirect a call or cause another failure, subject to calling rules, mapping permissions and enabled control-flow protections.

A C++ call selecting the appropriate virtual-function overrider from an object's dynamic type unless dispatch is suppressed or optimised away. Common ABIs implement dynamic dispatch with a virtual table; the C++ language does not require that representation.

A family of Clang control-flow integrity schemes, including type-based indirect-call and virtual-call checks. Most schemes require the documented LTO and visibility setup; other schemes such as kcfi have different requirements.

Link-time optimisation, which allows compiler analysis and optimisation across linked compilation units. Most Clang cfi sanitizer schemes require LTO; this is not a requirement of every control-flow protection.
Control-flow integrity that allows an indirect call only to functions whose type matches the call site. An attacker can still pick an unintended function of the same type.
A Windows forward-edge protection: the compiler inserts a check before indirect calls that the target is a valid function start, recorded in a bitmap. It is coarser than a type-based check.
A table with one bit per item recording yes or no. Microsoft CFG, for example, uses one to record which addresses are valid indirect-call targets.
Indirect Branch Tracking, part of Intel CET: when enabled, an indirect call or jump must land on an ENDBR64 (or ENDBR32) instruction, otherwise the CPU faults.

Branch Target Identification, introduced in Armv8.5-A: covered indirect branches into guarded pages must reach a compatible landing pad when checking is enabled. Accepted instructions and branch classes matter; some pointer-authentication instructions also serve as landing pads.
The x86-64 ENDBR instruction marking a valid indirect-branch target when Intel IBT checking applies. With IBT disabled it has no such checking effect; ENDBR32 is the distinct form for 32-bit code.

A marked location accepted by an enabled indirect-branch protection. Intel IBT uses ENDBR instructions; Arm BTI accepts compatible BTI instructions and some pointer-authentication instructions. Acceptance depends on branch class and configuration and does not establish an intended function type.

Control-flow Enforcement Technology: Intel processor features providing a hardware shadow stack (for returns) and Indirect Branch Tracking (for indirect calls and jumps); recent AMD processors also implement the shadow stack. Software, kernel and CPU must all support and enable it.

On supported x86 GCC targets, a flag requesting branch and return control-flow protection code and binary metadata. The full setting requests both; effective CET enforcement still requires compatible CPU, OS and runtime enablement.

Protected storage for copies of function return addresses. When enforcement covers a call and return, the return is checked against the protected copy; a mismatch faults instead of using the forged return address.

An Arm feature that adds and authenticates a keyed code for selected pointers using context. It authenticates rather than encrypts; coverage and finite authentication-code strength depend on configuration and it is not general memory safety.

Arm Memory Tagging Extension: suitably configured memory uses four-bit allocation tags for sixteen-byte granules, compared with logical pointer tags on checked accesses. Software must manage tags; mismatches can be reported synchronously or asynchronously, and matching tags or unchecked accesses can miss bugs.
example: Only under an independent uniform choice among all sixteen tags does one stale tag match with probability one in sixteen; allocator policies can differ.

definition: In MTE, a four-bit allocation value associated with a sixteen-byte granule or a logical value carried by a pointer. Software arranges tag assignment and retagging; freeing memory does not by itself guarantee that every stale pointer mismatches.
In MTE, the sixteen-byte region sharing one allocation tag. A boundary violation that remains within a granule with the matching tag is not identified by that tag comparison.

MTE reporting choices: synchronous checking reports a mismatch at the access; asynchronous checking can allow execution to continue before a later report. Linux also documents an asymmetric mode where available; enabled modes and costs depend on platform and workload.
Changes to a memory allocator that make heap bugs harder to exploit, such as protecting free-list pointers or delaying reuse of freed memory.

A glibc hardening mechanism for selected singly linked allocator lists that encodes links using address bits and also uses alignment checks. It constrains some pointer-corruption attacks but does not make all corruptions unusable or require a leak in every attack.

An allocator data structure tracking available blocks. Some implementations store links inside freed blocks, making those links targets for corruption; other structures and hardening choices are possible.

One Chromium raw_ptr implementation that tracks references for eligible allocations and holds freed storage while tracked references remain. Other raw_ptr implementations, unsupported allocations and untracked aliases have different coverage; it does not establish universal memory safety.

Memory mapped with permission to fetch and execute instructions. Stack and heap mappings are commonly non-executable, but actual permissions and JIT-generated executable mappings depend on platform policy.

An allocator making released storage available to a later object. A stale alias can then overlap new contents, but accessing an object outside its lifetime is invalid and C does not promise a particular observed value.

The compiler stage producing machine instructions from a program. Compiler-generated checks protect the covered generated operations; hand-written assembly, separately compiled code and runtime enablement can require separate arrangements.

A failure to convert between characters and bytes, for example an invalid multibyte or wide-character sequence. C's snprintf returns a negative value when one occurs, which is different from truncation.

The main release of Chrome and Chromium that ordinary users run, as opposed to the Beta, Dev and Canary test channels. Chromium's memory-safety statistics count security bugs that affected this release.
Failure to respect object bounds or lifetimes, or lack of checks preventing such failures. It includes spatial and temporal memory errors; it is the absence or violation of memory safety.

Text describing how a formatting function should produce output, including conversion directives and literal text. A fixed valid format is normal; letting untrusted input control it creates a separate format-string vulnerability.
An executable whose main image is not built as position independent. Conventional non-PIE ELF main code normally uses fixed addresses, even when other mappings are randomised.

In C, storage lasting for the execution of an associated block or call, with special lifetime rules for variable-length arrays. Automatic locals without an initializer have indeterminate values; static locals have different duration.
The limits of storage belonging to an object. An out-of-bounds access crosses those limits and may be a read or a write; mapped adjacent memory does not make it valid.

A control transfer whose target is obtained at run time rather than fixed directly in the instruction, including relevant indirect calls or jumps. The instruction class and target constraints depend on the architecture.
